precepts.text: He made himself strange unto them and spake roughly; Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him.
precepts.point: This does not prove the Israelites looked like the Egyptians; the peoples were all dark people. The change was his age, his dress, and the customs of the land he ruled in.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“And Joseph saw his brethren, and he knew them, but made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly unto them.” From the first meeting, “Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him.” He made himself strange on purpose, an Egyptian ruler asking a rough “Whence come ye?”

So when he finally says “I am Joseph”, they cannot answer him, troubled at his presence. They could not recognize their own brother. He was sold as a teenager and stood before them now a grown man in his years, and he had kept himself strange to them the whole time.

precepts.text: He spake unto them by an interpreter, though he understood every word.
precepts.point: This does not prove the Israelites looked like the Egyptians; the peoples were all dark people. The change was his age, his dress, and the customs of the land he ruled in.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“And they knew not that Joseph understood them; for he spake unto them by an interpreter.” Joseph understood every word his brethren said, but he spoke to them through an interpreter as any Egyptian lord would. That was part of the strangeness he put on: a man who needs an interpreter for the tongue of Canaan could not be their brother.

No wonder they were troubled at his presence when he spoke to them plainly, “I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?”

precepts.text: He shaved himself and changed his raiment; Joseph had taken on the customs of Egypt as second in command.
precepts.point: This does not prove the Israelites looked like the Egyptians; the peoples were all dark people. The change was his age, his dress, and the customs of the land he ruled in.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
When Pharaoh sent for him, “they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh.” From that day Joseph was clothed in the customs of Egypt: shaved, in Egyptian raiment, decked out as the second in command.

That is why his brethren could not know him. The change was his age, his dress, and the customs of the land he ruled in. It does not prove the Israelites looked like the Egyptians; the peoples were all dark people. It was the shaving, the raiment and the years that hid him.

precepts.text: Not until seven times, but until seventy times seven; the law of forgiveness Joseph showed his brethren.
precepts.point: The famine itself was called by the Most High, and the man was sent before them, even Joseph, sold for a servant, whose feet they hurt with fetters. The fetters and the iron are the prison where the king's prisoners were bound.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
Peter asked, “Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?” and Christ answered, “I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.” That is the law of forgiveness, and Joseph kept it. His own brothers sold him into slavery, and he told them, “be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life.”

That is the law Israel must keep with one another today: forgive thy brother, not until seven times, but until seventy times seven.

precepts.text: The patriarchs, moved with envy, sold Joseph into Egypt; but God was with him, delivered him out of all his afflictions, and made him governor.
precepts.point: The famine itself was called by the Most High, and the man was sent before them, even Joseph, sold for a servant, whose feet they hurt with fetters. The fetters and the iron are the prison where the king's prisoners were bound.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“And the patriarchs, moved with envy, sold Joseph into Egypt: but God was with him, And delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favour and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and he made him governor over Egypt and all his house.” Envy sold him; God was with him.

That is what Joseph told his brethren: “it was not you that sent me hither, but God: and he hath made me a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house, and a ruler throughout all the land of Egypt.” The Most High sent him before them to preserve life and to save the whole house of Israel by a great deliverance. Had he not been in Egypt, they would have died in the famine.

precepts.text: Touch not mine anointed; he called for a famine and sent a man before them, even Joseph, whose feet they hurt with fetters.
precepts.point: The famine itself was called by the Most High, and the man was sent before them, even Joseph, sold for a servant, whose feet they hurt with fetters. The fetters and the iron are the prison where the king's prisoners were bound.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“Saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm. Moreover he called for a famine upon the land: he brake the whole staff of bread. He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant: Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron.”

The famine itself was called by the Most High, and the man was sent before them, even Joseph. That is why Joseph could say “God did send me before you to preserve life”, and “it was not you that sent me hither, but God.” The selling for a servant, the fetters and the iron were all the road the Lord sent him down ahead of the famine to save his brethren’s lives by a great deliverance.

precepts.text: The fetters and the iron of the psalm are the prison where the king's prisoners were bound.
precepts.point: The famine itself was called by the Most High, and the man was sent before them, even Joseph, sold for a servant, whose feet they hurt with fetters. The fetters and the iron are the prison where the king's prisoners were bound.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“And Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound: and he was there in the prison.” The fetters and the iron of the psalm are this prison, the place where the king’s prisoners were bound.

That was part of the Most High sending him before them. From that prison Joseph went on to become a father to Pharaoh and lord of all his house, to preserve his brethren a posterity in the earth.

precepts.text: The word of the Lord tried him; the king loosed him and made him lord of his house, to teach his senators wisdom; then Israel also came into Egypt.
precepts.point: Jacob knew there was corn in Egypt because Joseph had already told Pharaoh exactly what to do to save up in the time of tribulation; when Jacob heard, he sent out the fathers. Applying these attributes makes better men, women, brothers, and sisters, to bring forth the nation unto the kingdom of God.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“Until the time that his word came: the word of the Lord tried him.” Joseph sat in the prison until the time that his word came; the word of the Lord tried him. Then “The king sent and loosed him; even the ruler of the people, and let him go free. He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance: To bind his princes at his pleasure; and teach his senators wisdom.”

That is who the brethren told Jacob about: “Joseph is yet alive, and he is governor over all the land of Egypt.” He was the teacher in Egypt, teaching Pharaoh’s senators wisdom, second in command, a king in all but title. Everything Egypt was at that point in time came through the influence of Joseph; the prosperity of that land was the favor the Lord had with Israel.

Then “Israel also came into Egypt; and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham. And he increased his people greatly; and made them stronger than their enemies.” That is Jacob’s answer here, “I will go and see him before I die”, and what came of it.

precepts.why:
“The Lord said, Verily it shall be well with thy remnant; verily I will cause the enemy to entreat thee well in the time of evil and in the time of affliction.” To go from prison to governor over all the land of Egypt is that favor. The Lord caused the enemy to entreat Joseph well in the time of his affliction, and it was well with him.

The same favor is promised to the remnant in the time of evil. It comes by keeping the commandments, as Joseph did.

precepts.why:
“For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same.” Joseph did that which is good, in Potiphar’s house and in the prison, and he had praise of the same: Pharaoh made him governor over all the land of Egypt.

Keep the commandments. A ruler is not a terror to good works, and the favor that lifted Joseph came by doing good under the power he was under.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation. Set thy heart aright, and constantly endure, and make not haste in time of trouble.” These are the characteristics of Joseph. He was tempted in Potiphar’s house and endured; he was put in prison and made not haste in the time of trouble. Do not be quick to leave the truth or find excuses in the time of trouble.

“Cleave unto him, and depart not away, that thou mayest be increased at thy last end. Whatsoever is brought upon thee take cheerfully, and be patient when thou art changed to a low estate.” Joseph was changed to a low estate, sold and imprisoned, and he was increased at his last end, governor over all the land of Egypt.

“For gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of adversity. Believe in him, and he will help thee; order thy way aright, and trust in him.” Joseph was gold tried in the fire, and the Lord helped him.

“Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.” Joseph began sold into slavery and put in prison under false pretenses. The end of the thing was governor of Egypt, a father to Pharaoh, with wagons sent to carry his father down. Better is the end than the beginning.

And he got there patient in spirit, not proud in spirit. The patient in spirit is better; that is what carried him from the beginning of the thing to its end.

“In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God also hath set the one over against the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him.” The Most High set the day of prosperity over against the day of adversity; Joseph had both, and Jacob had both, his heart fainting and then his spirit reviving at the sight of the wagons.

In the day of adversity consider the days that were good, and be patient in spirit. Consider means read the Bible more, study more, pray more, apply more. That is what the day of adversity is for.

“Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.” There is no other way into the kingdom but through tribulation. Our forefather Joseph went through it: the pit, the slavery, the prison, and then the governorship of Egypt.

When trials come, read the afflictions of the forefathers and the attributes they had in those times, and apply them: forgiveness, favor, righteousness, mercy. That is continuing in the faith through much tribulation.

But when Jacob heard that there was corn in Egypt, he sent out our fathers first.” Jacob knew there was corn in Egypt because Joseph had already told Pharaoh exactly what to do to save up in the time of tribulation; when Jacob heard, he sent out the fathers.

“And at the second time Joseph was made known to his brethren; and Joseph’s kindred was made known unto Pharaoh. When the Pharisees demanded when the kingdom of God should come, Christ answered, “The kingdom of God cometh not with observation: Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you.”

The kingdom is within, and it is brought forth by putting on these attributes of Joseph: forgiveness, favor, righteousness, mercy, patience in the day of adversity. Applying them makes better men, women, brothers and sisters, to bring forth the nation unto the kingdom of God.
